summary: Work that keeps running with no end date, such as a service you provide every day.
example: Collection Service, which moves produce from every depot to the buyer, every day of the season.
definition: An operation is continuing work with no end date: a service the organisation runs day in and day out, or one it has decided on and is setting up (planned), or one it has stopped (retired) (TAXONOMY.md, the definitions; D14). The first question about any work is whether it ends: work that ends is a project or a programme, work that keeps running is an operation. An operation carries the name of the service (D17); a project that sets it up or changes it is named for that change, hands over to it, and the operation's team accepts the handover. It has a service owner, the role accountable for it end to end (ITIL), and a team that runs it (D23, D27). Its service levels are watched through indicators. Business as usual sits inside a programme's boundary, so an operation names the programmes it is part of, if any (D2). An operation is not a project (it has no closure), not a team (the team runs it; the operation is the service), and not a data source (a source is where records are kept; an operation may read or produce them). Its checks advise and never block.

cues.operation: a service or routine that runs every day, week or month

/metadata/name.guide: The name of the service, as the people who use it would say it. The service keeps its name; a project that changes it is named for the change.

poor.why: Names a change that ends, which is a project landing in the service, not the service itself.
Names the team that runs the service, not the service.

/spec/purpose.guide: What the service does, day in and day out, and what for, in one sentence. It describes continuing work: no end date, no target figure.
good: Check every delivery for quality and route failures into rework.
Move produce from every depot to the buyer within a day of intake.
Keep one record per member, current enough to pay, count and contact them from.

poor.text: Introduce quality checks at every depot by the end of 2026.
poor.why: Work that ends: introducing the checks is a project that hands over to this service.
A target, not what the service does: the figure belongs to an indicator.
A topic, not a service: say what it does and for whom.

/spec/status.guide: Where the service is in its life. Planned: decided on and being set up, not yet run; the project that sets it up names it and hands it over. Running: in use today, which is how a service already running is recorded when it is first brought into Cartograph. Retired: no longer offered.

/spec/serviceOwner.guide: The role accountable for the service end to end (ITIL's service owner), from the Resource catalogue. It is the role that accepts a project's handover into the service. A role, never a person; when no role fits, define the role first.

poor.why: A person, not a role: Cartograph names roles, and people hold them.
A team, which goes in the team field; the service owner is one accountable role.

/spec/team.guide: The team that runs the service, from the team tree. It decides whose work the operation is. When no team fits, define the team first.

poor.why: A role, not a team: the role accountable goes in the service owner.

/spec/serviceWindow.guide: The hours and days the service runs, plainly enough that a user knows when they can rely on it.
good: Daily through the season, reduced rounds out of season.

poor.why: Nobody can plan around it: say when the service runs.
Dates with an end describe a project; an operation keeps running.

/spec/programmes.guide: The programmes this service is part of. Name one only when the programme coordinates this service towards its change; an operation outside any programme is normal, and nothing advises against it. The programme reads its components back from here.

poor.text: market-access-programme, because the same team works on it
poor.why: Sharing a team or a stakeholder is the portfolio test failing, not membership: name a programme only when it steers this service towards its change.

/spec/kpis.guide: The indicators that say whether the service is running at the level it should: its service levels, from the KPI register. When none exists, define the KPI first.

poor.why: Measures a benefit of the wider strategy, which this service only contributes to; a service level says how the service itself performs.

/spec/data.guide: The service's two-way relationship with data: what it reads, and what it creates or adds to, with where that lands.

/spec/data/consumes/-/source.guide: A data source the service reads and never writes back to, from the data source register.

/spec/data/consumes/-/purpose.guide: What the service uses the data for, in one sentence.
good: Identify members with deliveries due for a check this season.

poor.why: Says what the data is, not what the service does with it.

/spec/data/consumes/-/handoff.guide: How the data reaches the service: a feed, a file transfer, a shared database, manual re-entry or paper.

/spec/data/consumes/-/personalData.guide: Whether the data used holds personal data, sensitive personal data, or none.

/spec/data/produces/-/output.guide: What the service puts into the world: records in an existing source, documents or files, an extract or report, or a new data source.

/spec/data/produces/-/sink.guide: Where the produced data lands: the register, system or store that holds it afterwards.

/spec/data/produces/-/purpose.guide: What the produced data is for, in one sentence.
good: Record quality check results for each delivery.

poor.why: Says nothing about what is recorded or why.

/spec/data/produces/-/refresh.guide: How often the data is brought up to date where it lands.

/spec/data/produces/-/personalData.guide: Whether the produced data holds personal data, sensitive personal data, or none.

/spec/mandate.guide: What requires or authorises the service: a decision, policy, law or regulation, contract, business case or request, each with its title and, where there is one, its reference, date and issuing body.

/spec/mandate/-/title.guide: The title of the decision or document, as it is written.

poor.why: Habit is not a mandate: leave the mandate empty, or name the decision or policy that requires the service.

/spec/mandate/-/issuedBy.guide: The body that issued it, never a person.

/spec/notes.guide: Anything a reader needs that has no field of its own. Not a place for what a field already holds.

Project:/spec/operation.ask: Which project sets this service up, or changes it?
Project:/spec/operation.ifNone: For a planned service, start the project that sets it up, naming this service as where it lands. A running service needs none until something about it has to change.

checks.service-purpose: Say what the service does, day in and day out.
checks.service-owner: Name the role accountable for the service end to end as its service owner, from the Resource catalogue.
checks.service-hours: Give the hours and days the service runs.
checks.alignment-programmes: Name a programme only when the service is one of its components; an operation outside any programme needs nothing here.
checks.measures-kpis: Name at least one indicator that shows the service's level.
checks.service-status: A planned service is set up by a project that names it as where it lands; once that project hands over, mark the service running.
